phonemes.desc: The pinyin h is the velar fricative [x] — the 'ch' of Scottish 'loch', not an English h; the diphthong glides [u→a] into the velar nasal [ŋ], 'ng' as in 'sing', all on the second tone: a rising glide, ˧˥.
Voiceless unaspirated [t] — the 't' of 'stay' — on high front [i]; the fourth tone falls hard through the register, ˥˩, like a door closing: apt for 帝, 'sovereign, thearch.'

pronunciation.approximation: 'HWAHNG-dee' — 'hwang' rising as though the syllable itself were climbing, 'dee' dropping decisively: rise, then fall.

kin.label: Traditional
kin.form: 黃帝 Huángdì — 黃 'yellow' + 帝 'sovereign'; not 皇帝 huángdì 'emperor,' a modern homophone, a different word.

kin.label: Personal name
kin.form: 軒轅 Xuānyuán, 'Chariot-Axle' — the name the Shiji gives him, later a byword for the Yellow Emperor.

kin.label: Clan name
kin.form: 有熊氏 Yǒuxióng shì, the Bear clan of which he was born head; the Shiji also gives him the surname 公孫 Gōngsūn.

kin.label: Paired ancestor
kin.form: 炎帝 Yándì, the Flame Emperor — his defeated rival at Banquan, afterward his twin in 炎黃子孫, 'descendants of Yán and Huáng.' A pair, never one figure.

pronunciation.note: Huángdì is Tier 1 because tone is lexical: the acute á and the grave ì carry the second and fourth citation tones, and in Mandarin tone is meaning — mā 'mother,' má 'hemp,' mǎ 'horse,' mà 'scold.' The plain ASCII 'huangdi' flattens both contours to silence. (And 黃帝 'Yellow Emperor' and 皇帝 'emperor' romanize identically — only the characters keep them apart.)

domains.title: The Yellow Emperor
domains.subtitle: Founding Sovereign, First Ancestor, and Giver of Civilization
domains.lead: Huángdì — the Yellow Emperor, Xuānyuán of the Bear clan — is the founding ancestor the Chinese tradition gave itself: the sovereign who won the land at Banquan and Zhuolu, ordered the calendar and the script, and rode a yellow dragon up to Heaven when his work was done. A culture-hero of the late Warring States imagination, he became what the Shiji made him: the first of the Five Emperors, ancestor of all who call themselves children of Yán and Huáng.

cards.name: The Founder at Arms
cards.desc: Three victories at Banquan over the Flame Emperor Yándì, then the great battle at Zhuolu where Chīyóu fell — the two wars by which the Shiji says the realm was first united (Shiji 1).

cards.name: First Ancestor
cards.desc: 炎黃子孫 yánhuáng zǐsūn, 'descendants of Yán and Huáng' — the name a fifth of humanity calls itself; his tomb at Qiaoshan is honored as the ancestral root of the entire people.

cards.name: Giver of the Arts
cards.desc: Writing by his scribe Cāng Jié, the sixty-year cycle by Dà Náo, the twelve pitch-pipes by Líng Lún, silk by his wife Léi Zǔ, medicine in his dialogues with Qí Bó — civilization chartered in one reign.

cards.name: The Model of Rule
cards.desc: The golden-age sovereign: 'he made the officials by the clouds and the hosts by the signs' — the template every dynasty measured itself against, the face on the Huáng-Lǎo school's banner.

symbols.name: The Yellow Dragon
symbols.meaning: At the end of his reign a dragon descended to carry him to Heaven (Shiji 28) — the animal that is China itself, come to fetch the man who made it; 'descendants of the dragon' is the people's other name.

symbols.name: The color yellow and the Center
symbols.meaning: In five-phase cosmology yellow belongs to the Earth phase and the center of space — the axis he holds among the Five Emperors; dynasties claimed imperial yellow as his inheritance.

symbols.name: The clouds as emblem
symbols.meaning: The Shiji says he 'took the clouds as his emblem and named his officers from the clouds' — Heaven's weather turned into a ministry, the first charter of bureaucracy.

symbols.name: The south-pointing chariot
symbols.meaning: Later tradition credits him with the zhǐnánchē, the compass cart said to have led his army out of the fog Chīyóu raised at Zhuolu — a magnetic legend, whatever its date.

symbols.name: Bears, tigers, and the war-beasts
symbols.meaning: For Zhuolu he 'tamed bears, brown bears, leopards, and tigers' to fight for him (Shiji 1) — the culture-hero as master of the wild; his clan name is the Bear (Yǒuxióng).

symbols.name: The precious tripod
symbols.meaning: He 'obtained the precious tripod and calculated the sun with counting-rods' (Shiji 1), and cast a great cauldron from Shoushan copper (Shiji 28) — the dǐng as emblem of legitimate rule, carried on by the nine tripods of Yǔ.

symbols.name: Mount Qiao (橋山 Qiáoshān)
symbols.meaning: His tomb in Huangling County, Shaanxi — the First Tomb Under Heaven — said to hold not his body, snatched up by the dragon, but his bow, cap, and clothes.

mythology.lead: The Yellow Emperor is the archaeologist's dream of a beginning: warlord, inventor, lawgiver, and immortal in one. Sīmǎ Qiān's Shǐjì (ch. 1) gives him his biography; the Zhuāngzǐ gives him his soul. Between the two stands the mythic sovereign — victorious at Banquan and Zhuolu, ordering all the arts of life, and refusing to die in the ordinary way.

myths.title: Xuānyuán of the Bear Clan
myths.text: “The Yellow Emperor was a son of Shǎodiǎn, surnamed Gōngsūn, and his name was Xuānyuán.” So the Shiji opens the first reign of Chinese history (ch. 1): born head of the Yǒuxióng, the Bear clan, praised in the formula of sage-birth legend — “born divine, he spoke early, and as an infant was quick-witted” — and handed an army, not a cradle. Modern scholarship reads the story plainly: not an excavable biography but a Warring States and Han construction, its earliest layers barely older than the fourth century BCE. The tradition never asked to be believed as chronicle, only honored as charter.

myths.title: Banquan and Zhuolu
myths.text: The founding required two victories. First, three battles at Banquan, after which “the hosts of the world gave allegiance to him where the Flame Emperor was concerned” (Shiji 1): Yándì, defeated, became not an enemy but the first subject — and, in time, the twin ancestor beside him. Then the great battle: Chīyóu of the Jiǔlí raised a fog over the field at Zhuolu, and the army lost its way — later tradition answered with the south-pointing chariot that always faced south, however the carriage turned. The Shiji compresses the war into one sentence of terrible calm: he “waged battle with Chīyóu at Zhuolu and captured and killed him.” Banquan made him sovereign of the willing; Zhuolu made him sovereign of the wild.

myths.title: The Charter of Civilization
myths.text: What the Shiji celebrates most is not conquest but administration — a single reign made to carry the list of inventions. “He took the clouds as his emblem and named his officers from the clouds” — the first bureaucracy. He obtained the precious tripod and “calculated the sun with counting-rods”; his chronologer Dà Náo fixed the sixty-year cycle of stems and branches that still names traditional years. His music-master Líng Lún tuned the twelve pitch-pipes in the valley of Xiédù; his wife Léi Zǔ taught the rearing of silkworms, and silk clothed an empire. His historian Cāng Jié invented writing — and the Huáinánzǐ attaches to the deed one of the most haunting sentences in Chinese myth: “when Cāng Jié invented writing, grain rained from Heaven and the ghosts wailed at night.” The Shiji's list is the charter every guild of inventors shared.

myths.title: The Dragon at Jīngshān
myths.text: No hero of this size is allowed an ordinary death. Tradition credits him with a century of rule; then, the Shiji says (ch. 28), he cast a great cauldron from Shǒushān copper beneath Mount Jīng — and when it was finished, a dragon descended, beard trailing low, to carry him up. He mounted with seventy of his officers and households; those who could not climb seized his bow and his robe, and the dragon rose anyway. The bow and clothes they buried at Mount Qiao — which, the Shiji explains, is why the tomb on Qiaoshan stands though no body lies in it. The myth is the hinge of his cult: a sovereign who ascends is a sovereign who watches. Every dynasty that offered at his tomb was filing a report with the founder.

myths.title: Guǎngchéngzǐ of Mount Kōngtóng (Zhuangzi 11)
myths.text: The Zhuāngzǐ keeps a second, older Yellow Emperor — not the inventor of everything but the man who had to be unmade. Desiring to govern all under Heaven well, Xuānyuán went up Mount Kōngtóng to ask Guǎngchéngzǐ about the essence of the great Way. The first interview failed: “you govern all under Heaven, and see that the clouds do not gather before they should rain, the trees shed their leaves before they turn yellow, the sun and moon give light more and more dimly — a mind like yours is unfit to speak of the great Way.” The Emperor went away, gave up the throne, built a solitary hut, and fasted from inquiry for three months. When he returned, Guǎngchéngzǐ taught him: keep the essence of your complete being, guard the One, live twelve hundred years without decline. The story is the Daoist canon at its most subversive: the sovereign must shed sovereignty to find what sovereignty is for — the maker of the state taught by the man who refused it.

myths.title: Xuānyuán and the Dark Pearl (Zhuangzi 12)
myths.text: In another Zhuangzi parable (ch. 12) Xuānyuán, wandering north of the Red Waters, lost his dark pearl — the xuánzhū, the mysterious pearl of the Way. He sent Knowledge to find it; Knowledge could not. He sent keen-eyed Sight; Sight could not. He sent quick-tongued Discourse; Discourse could not. At last he sent Formless-and-Actionless, xiàngwǎng — and xiàngwǎng found it. The parable is the whole Zhuangzi in miniature: the man whose reign organized knowledge, sight, and words into instruments of state learns that the pearl of the Way is recovered only by the one who stops grasping. The emperor who named every office bows to the nameless.

lore.syncretism: Huángdì's true temple is a library — the most syncretic figure in the Chinese canon, claimed by every school that needed a founder. The Zhuāngzǐ made him the philosophical sovereign who must unlearn rule; the early Han made him a political program: the Huáng-Lǎo 黃老 school, “the Yellow Emperor and Lǎozǐ,” which guided the recovered economy of Emperors Wén and Jǐng, and whose lost scriptures — the Four Classics of the Yellow Emperor, recovered from the Mawangdui silk library in 1973 — show how literally the school took him as lawgiver. The medical tradition made him a student: the Huángdì Nèijīng casts its whole science as his interrogation of the physician Qí Bó. And the people made him a pair: with the Flame Emperor he forms the twin root 炎黃 — rivals at Banquan, brothers in the bloodline.
lore.culturalLegacy: The name 炎黃子孫 — “descendants of Yán and Huáng” — is his living monument: the self-designation of the Chinese people in the twentieth century and beyond. His second is the Huángdì Nèijīng 黃帝內經, the Inner Canon of the Yellow Emperor: a Han compilation in the Suwen and Lingshu books, cast as dialogues between the sovereign and Qí Bó, and still the foundational text of traditional Chinese medicine — perhaps the only medical classic framed as debate between ruler and physician. Imperial yellow — reserved to the throne from Tang times onward — took its sanction from his name. Modernity keeps re-engraving him: 軒轅 Xuānyuán is a personal name again, and the Xuānyuánjiàn 軒轅劍 game series carries the founder's name into global entertainment.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Every civilization invents its own beginning; the Chinese invention is unusually honest about what it is doing. The Yellow Emperor is not a memory of a man — the scholarly consensus is firm — but a theory of what a beginning should be: a single reign in which war was won, writing invented, the calendar fixed, music tuned, silk taught, and the ruler carried to Heaven on a dragon rather than buried like the rest of us. The Shiji's chapter on him is a constitution disguised as a chronicle.

It is fitting that his name is exactly where Mandarin's distinctive feature lives. Tone is not decoration on Huángdì; it is the difference between the Yellow Emperor and a noise. The tradition that credits him with the invention of writing knew what this project also knows: orthography is the foundation of the Way. To write Huángdì — rising á, falling ì — is to keep the founder's name the way the Shiji kept his reign: completely, and on purpose.

lore.archaeology: Mount Qiao in Huangling County, Shaanxi, is the material anchor: a tomb-mound said to hold only the Yellow Emperor's bow, cap, and robes, honored as the First Tomb Under Heaven. The earliest secure state visit recorded is Emperor Wu of Han's northern tour of 110 BCE, when the Shiji (ch. 28) has him pause to offer at the tomb on Qiaoshan — though the same chapter shows the age already puzzled by how a man who ascended on a dragon came to have a grave. The honest caveat is essential: no archaeological culture can be securely identified with the Yellow Emperor, and identifications of his people with this or that Neolithic horizon — Yangshao and its cousins — are conjectures driven by the myth more than by the trowel. What is genuinely ancient is the address of the cult: a real mountain in the loess of Shaanxi, pointed at by texts two thousand years old.
lore.cult: The Yellow Emperor's cult is the ancestral cult of an entire people. The tomb at Qiaoshan drew recorded imperial attention from Emperor Wu of Han's offering in 110 BCE onward, and the rite became a spring observance. The modern state made it national: in 1912 the infant Republic sent a delegation of fifteen to sacrifice at the tomb and proclaim the Yellow Emperor the ancestor of the whole nation; in 1937 the Qingming rites became a rare joint act of Kuomintang and Communists, for which both governments published sacrificial odes — the most famous the Ji Huangdi Ling Wen issued in Mao Zedong's name. Since 2008 the People's Republic has held formal public ancestor rites at the mausoleum on Qingming itself, with Taiwanese delegations and diaspora associations maintaining parallel observances. The liturgy has changed dynasty by dynasty; the addressee has not.
lore.iconography: No image of the Yellow Emperor predates the Han, and the image everyone knows is imperial projection: the yellow-robed, dragon-throned sovereign is the iconography of Tang and Ming emperors read backward onto the founder — a process the Han began, when funerary shrines carved galleries of ancient sovereigns. The Wu Liang shrine's stone reliefs (Shandong, 151 CE) are the great surviving cycle of the culture-heroes, and scholars generally include a Yellow Emperor among its ancient rulers, though the panels' identifications are reconstructed and should be claimed cautiously. The modern mausoleum completes the type in bronze — the great seated statue at Qiaoshan is a twentieth-century imperial icon wearing a third-millennium name. He is less a portrait than a throne: whatever century imagines him, it imagines itself sitting in it.
lore.reception: The Zhuangzi's philosophical Yellow Emperor — the ruler taught by Guangchengzi, the loser of the dark pearl found only by the imageless one — is his earliest and most subversive afterlife, and the seed of the Huáng-Lǎo synthesis that governed the early Han in his name and Laozi's together. The medical canon gave him a second: for two thousand years every physician of the Chinese tradition has learned his art as the Yellow Emperor's questions to Qibo, so that his name opens the first page of East Asia's medicine as Hippocrates' opens the West's. The modern era turned him into the nation: Sun Yat-sen's 1912 delegation, the joint KMT–CCP rites of 1937, and the restored ceremonies at Qiaoshan from 2008 forward all rest on one foundation — the claim that the children of Yán and Huáng are one family, addressed by one name. He began as a Han dynasty charter; he has never stopped being read.
